prompt: A 4-core server CPU runs at 2.5 GHz. Each core sustains two 512-bit float32 FMAs per cycle at that clock. What is its theoretical peak single-precision throughput?

options.explanation: Correct. Each core sustains 64 FLOPs per cycle. Four such cores at 2.5 billion cycles per second give 640 billion FLOPs per second.
This forgets that each FMA counts as two FLOPs.
This uses only one FMA unit and counts each FMA as one FLOP.
This double-counts something: 512-bit registers hold 16 floats, not 32.

workedExample:
Build it up from one lane to the whole chip:

```formula
L = 512 / 32 = 16
F_cyc = N_u L F_op
F_cyc = 2 × 16 × 2 = 64
F_peak = N_c f_clk F_cyc
F_peak = 4 × 2.5 × 10^9 Hz × 64
F_peak = 640 × 10^9 FLOP/s
where
L: float32 lanes in a 512-bit register
F_cyc: FLOPs per cycle per core
N_u: FMA units per core; 2
F_op: FLOPs per FMA lane; 2 (multiply and add)
F_peak: the chip's peak, in FLOPs per second
N_c: the number of cores; 4
f_clk: the clock frequency, in hertz (Hz); 2.5 GHz = 2.5 × 10^9 Hz
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
FLOP/s: floating-point operations per second; 640 × 10^9 FLOP/s = 640 GFLOP/s
In words: 64 FLOPs per cycle per core, times 4 cores, times 2.5 billion cycles a second, is 640 GFLOP/s.
```

This is an arithmetic ceiling. Approaching it requires enough independent FMAs and data supply while sustaining the stated clock; other instructions may issue concurrently.

prompt: Profiling shows 70% of a program's time is in a loop. You vectorise it with AVX and the loop itself runs exactly 8× faster. Assume the remaining work and all overhead are unchanged. What is the overall speedup?

options.explanation: Only the loop speeds up; the other 30% of the time is unchanged.
This multiplies 0.7 by 8, which is not how speedups combine.
That is the limit 1 / 0.3 if the loop took zero time, not the 8× case.

workedExample:
Amdahl's law applies to any partial speedup:

```formula
S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f / k)
S = 1 / (0.3 + 0.7 / 8)
S = 1 / (0.3 + 0.0875) = 1 / 0.3875
S ≈ 2.58
where
S: the overall speedup of the program
f: the fraction of time in the vectorised loop; 0.7
k: how many times faster the loop becomes; 8
≈: approximately equal to
In words: an 8× faster loop that is 70% of the time makes the whole program only about 2.6× faster.
```

Even infinite vector width would only give 1 / 0.3 ≈ 3.3×. To go further, look at the remaining 30%.
